name: Illusion of transparency
statement: People overestimate how far their inner states leak out, so a lie, a rush of nerves or a flash of disgust feels visible to a room that mostly cannot see it.
meaning: The claim compares two quantities. One is how strongly a person feels something, the other is how much of it another person can actually read off their face and voice. The gap opens because the feeling is the most vivid thing in its owner's head, and the correction for the fact that nobody else has access to it is too small. Gilovich, Savitsky and Medvec call that anchoring on one's own experience and adjusting too little. A design can only test it by measuring the belief and the reality in the same room, which is why the paradigms all pair a performer with observers who are questioned separately.

origin.who: Thomas Gilovich, Kenneth Savitsky and Victoria Husted Medvec
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their paper is "The illusion of transparency: Biased assessments of others' ability to read one's emotional states", and it named the effect and set out the anchoring account.

evidence: The 1998 paper reports three sets of studies. Its abstract at the publisher says liars overestimate the detectability of their lies in Studies 1a, 1b and 1c, that people believe their feelings of disgust are more apparent than they are in Studies 2a and 2b, and that Studies 3a and 3b carry the idea into people's reluctance to intervene in emergencies. All three sets are read by the authors as insufficient adjustment from the anchor of one's own phenomenological experience. The full text is paywalled and could not be obtained for this entry, so its sample sizes and the percentages usually quoted from the trivia-game lying studies are left out rather than repeated. Savitsky and Gilovich extended the idea to public speaking in 2003, and that paper is available here at the same level of detail. Its abstract says Study 1 documents that nervous speakers believe their nervousness is more apparent to the audience than it is, and that Study 2 shows an awareness of the illusion improves a speaker's performance, judged both by the speaker and by observers. The publisher's summary of Study 1 says participants delivered extemporaneous speeches in pairs, then rated how nervous they themselves had appeared and how nervous their counterpart had appeared.

replication.headline: Independent samples reproduce the gap between felt and visible nerves, while two unpublished theses failed on the lying version and on the speech-anxiety remedy.
replication.detail: MacInnis, Mackinnon and MacIntyre ran the speech comparison in a live classroom instead of in pairs, and describe it as a conceptual replication of the 2003 study. Students in an introductory public speaking course spoke to audiences averaging 15.0 people. Speakers rated their own anxiety, rated the speech again from the imagined view of the audience, and the audience rated them on the adapted scale. Imagined audience ratings averaged 23.3 against actual audience ratings of 17.3, t(91) = 7.89, p < .001. Speakers' own anxiety averaged 24.0 and also ran above the audience, t(92) = 7.71, p < .001. Trait public speaking anxiety tracked the size of the gap, r(65) = .37, p < .001. One result cut against the mechanism: 36% of speakers thought the audience saw more anxiety than they had felt, which is not anxiety leaking out. Rai, Mitchell and Faelling had participants read true and false episodic memories to an audience, and their abstract reports that speakers overestimated both how many listeners would think they were the liar and how many would pick the liar correctly. Their second experiment found listeners could separate lies from truths, with error. Rai, Mitchell, Kadar and Mackenzie report the same overconfidence in 13 and 14 year olds and in adults who described and lied about pictures, with adolescents no more egocentric than adults. Two unpublished theses go the other way. Mandelbaum's dissertation ran three experiments with children, adolescents and undergraduates making true and false statements, and its abstract reports the illusion when participants told the truth and not when they lied. Gloth screened 543 students for fear of negative evaluation, brought back the top quartile, and had 31 of them give a three-minute speech after being informed about the illusion, reassured, or given no instruction. Her abstract reports results not consistent with previous research, which is a failure of the 2003 remedy rather than of the illusion.

study.cite: MacInnis, C. C., Mackinnon, S. P., & MacIntyre, P. D. (2010). The illusion of transparency and normative beliefs about anxiety during public speaking. Current Research in Social Psychology, 15(4), 42-52.

limits: The search behind this verdict covered Crossref, PubMed, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, the publisher pages for both founding papers, and web searches for preregistered, multi-laboratory and registered-report replications. No Many Labs project and no registered report on this effect came up. Neither founding paper is open access and every hosted copy located was refused by its server, so the entry rests on publisher abstracts for the 1998 and 2003 studies and quotes no number from either. No standardised effect size is reported in anything reachable, and none is calculated here. The abstract of the 2014 adolescent study was read through Semantic Scholar's record rather than at Springer, which served only the reference list. The two dissenting results are a master's thesis and a doctoral dissertation, neither peer reviewed, and the thesis rested on 31 speakers. Brown and Stopa took a different route, asking participants to rate both illusions after a memory task under low and high social evaluation, and found transparency rated above the spotlight effect in the low condition and the order reversed in the high one. That measures how the two feelings move, not the distance between belief and reality, so it is not a test of the gap.
misreadings: The effect is not the spotlight effect. The spotlight effect is about how much others notice one's actions and appearance; this is about how much they can read one's inner state. Gilovich and Savitsky set the pair side by side in 1999 as two egocentric assessments, and Brown and Stopa found them moving in opposite directions as social pressure rose. The finding is also passed on as an assurance that nothing shows at all. Rai and colleagues report that listeners could tell lies from truths, so the honest summary is overestimation rather than invisibility. The therapeutic version runs ahead of the evidence in the same way. Savitsky and Gilovich's Study 2 found that telling speakers about the illusion improved their speeches, and the one attempt to repeat that, on 31 speakers selected for fear of negative evaluation, did not.
